6Career Families, Broadly

Instead of picking one narrow job title, it is more useful to notice which broad family keeps pulling at you. Think of these as neighbourhoods, and you are exploring which one feels like home.

Creative careers

Design, writing, photography, video, music, art direction, content creation. These involve making things that communicate or express. Good for people who value originality and visual or verbal expression. Honest note: they can be competitive and income may vary, especially at the start, so building a portfolio matters.

Technology careers

Software development, data analysis, IT support, cybersecurity, product management, automation. These involve building or maintaining digital systems. Good for people who like logic, problem-solving and continuous learning. Honest note: tools change quickly, so you need to keep learning.

Business careers

Operations, sales, marketing, finance, accounting, human resources, project management. These involve running and growing organisations. Good for people who like organisation, people and results. Honest note: roles vary hugely, so research specific job descriptions.

People-focused careers

Teaching, coaching, counselling, nursing and other healthcare roles, social work, customer success, community work. These involve helping, guiding and supporting people. Good for people who value empathy and impact. Honest note: they can be emotionally demanding, and many require specific qualifications and registration, so check requirements early.

Analytical careers

Research, data and policy analysis, strategy, planning, economics. These involve studying information to answer questions and support decisions. Good for people who like detail, patterns and evidence.

Practical and trade careers

Construction, electrical work, plumbing, hairdressing, cooking, tailoring, mechanics, agriculture, logistics. These involve skilled hands-on work. Good for people who like tangible results and practical problem-solving. Honest note: they are often in strong demand and can offer excellent independence, but they may be physically demanding and have apprenticeship or licensing routes.

Flexible and independent careers

Freelancing, consulting, running a small business. These involve working for yourself, often combining other skills. Good for people who value independence. Honest note: income can be uneven and you must handle your own sales and admin. See How To Get Your First Freelance Client.

These families overlap

A great marketer is creative and analytical. A great nurse is practical and people-focused. A great freelancer is independent and business-minded. Do not force yourself into one box. Use these families as a way to notice patterns, not as labels.

A short exercise

Look back at your fit profile. Which two families appear most? Write them at the top of a page. Those are where you will start exploring.

7Remote Work Versus In-Person Work

Neither is better. They suit different people and different seasons of life.

Remote work means you do your job from home or anywhere with internet. It can offer flexibility, no commute and wider job choices. It rewards self-direction, clear written communication and comfort with less daily social contact. It can feel lonely, and it needs boundaries so work does not swallow your home life.

In-person work means you go to a workplace. It often offers structure, immediate feedback, built-in social contact and a clear end to the day. It may be less flexible about your time and place.

Hybrid work mixes the two.

Ask yourself honestly which fits your personality, your home situation and your season of life. Not which sounds more impressive. If you are curious about remote careers, read 10 Remote Online Jobs That Can Grow Toward $5,000 A Month.

8Career Growth And Job Demand

A field with almost no demand makes even a perfect fit harder to turn into income. So before going all-in on a direction, do a short reality check.

The fifteen-minute demand check

1. Search the career title plus "jobs" or "hiring" in your location, and then for remote roles. 2. Look at how many listings appear and how often they are posted. 3. Read five job descriptions. Note the required skills, qualifications and experience. 4. Note any pay information, bearing in mind that figures may be estimates. 5. Check a national or official labour statistics website for your country, if one exists, for information about demand and typical pay.

You are looking for evidence that real employers or clients pay for this work. This is not about chasing only popular fields. It is about not planning your life around a market that has quietly shrunk.

Think about direction, not just today

Ask: Is this field growing, steady or shrinking? Will technology change it, and how? Is there a path to progress, such as junior to senior? What skills would keep me valuable? You will not know for sure, but asking these questions prevents surprises. For help with the skills that tend to hold value, see Best Money-Making Skills To Learn In 2026.

A caution about hype

Be careful with lists of "highest paying jobs" and glamorous career videos. Many leave out how long training takes, how competitive entry is and what the daily reality is like. Treat them as inspiration, never as proof.

9Transferable Skills Matter More Than You Think

A transferable skill is an ability that works in many jobs. Communication, organisation, problem-solving, reliability, learning quickly, teaching, persuading, handling money, working with people and managing time are all transferable.

This matters because most career changes are not starting over. They are moving what you already have into a new setting.

Find yours

Look at your past work, study, volunteering and home life. For each, write three things you did, then translate them into skills.

What I didThe skill hiding inside it
Managed a small shop's till and stockHandling money, accuracy, customer service, inventory
Organised my church or community eventPlanning, coordination, leadership, budgeting
Looked after younger siblingsPatience, teaching, responsibility, conflict handling
Helped friends with their CVsWriting, editing, understanding what employers want
Ran a small online side hustleMarketing, sales, customer communication
Studied a hard subject alongside workDiscipline, time management, learning quickly

Using them in applications

When you apply for a role in a new area, show how your transferable skills solve their problem. "At my previous job I handled forty customer enquiries a day, which means I am comfortable with fast written communication" is stronger than "I am a good communicator."

Gaps are fillable

If you find a gap between your current skills and a career you want, that is a plan, not a verdict. The question becomes: what would it take to close this gap, how long and at what cost? We cover that below.

10How To Explore A Career Properly

Most people try to decide a career by thinking. The best method is to research, talk and test. Here is how.

Step one: research the basics

For each career you are curious about, find answers to these questions from reliable sources:

  • What does a person in this role actually do on a normal day?
  • What skills and qualifications are needed?
  • How long does it take to qualify, and what does it cost?
  • What is typical pay, and what range exists?
  • Where do people work, and what are the hours like?
  • How do people progress?
  • What do people find hardest about it?

Good sources include official careers websites for your country, professional association pages, job descriptions and written or video interviews with people in the role.

Step two: read real job descriptions

A job description lists what an employer wants. Read five for each career. Highlight repeated skills and phrases. If many listings ask for something you have never heard of, you have found a learning goal.

Step three: talk to real people

This is the most powerful step, and most beginners skip it. An informational interview is a short, friendly conversation where you ask someone about their work, not for a job. Most people are happy to help, because they enjoy being asked about their experience.

Who to ask: people you know, friends of friends, tutors, community contacts and professionals you reach through LinkedIn or alumni networks. Questions to ask:

  • What does a normal week look like?
  • What do you enjoy most and least about the work?
  • What surprised you when you started?
  • What skills matter most?
  • How did you get started?
  • What would you tell someone who wants to enter this field?
  • Is there anyone else you suggest I speak to?

Keep it to fifteen to twenty minutes. Say thank you. Follow up with a short note.

Step four: test it in small, cheap ways

You do not have to commit to a three-year course to find out whether you like something. Try a small experiment: a short online course, a weekend workshop, volunteering for a few hours, shadowing someone for a day, a practice project, a short freelance task or an entry-level job in the field. The purpose is not to prove you will be great. It is to learn whether you like the daily reality.

Step five: reflect

After each experiment, write down: What did I enjoy? What drained me? What surprised me? Would I want more of this? Your reflections will reveal more than any quiz. Keep them in one note so you can compare options over time.

11Ten Career Snapshots To Make The Options Real

Sometimes the hardest part is that you cannot picture the work. So here are ten snapshots of common beginner-friendly careers. Each one says what the person does, how people often enter, which of your six lenses it tends to suit and what to be honest about. They are starting points for your own research, not a recommendation list. Entry routes, pay and demand differ a great deal between countries, so check what applies where you live.

Administrative assistant or office coordinator

What they do. Keep an office running: answer messages, manage calendars, organise files, prepare documents, welcome visitors, order supplies and support the team.

How people enter. Often through entry-level roles, temporary work or a short administrative course. Comfort with email, documents and spreadsheets matters a great deal. See Digital Skills For Beginners.

Often suits. People who value stability, enjoy order and like helping others succeed.

Be honest about. The work can be repetitive and pay at entry level is usually modest, but it is a strong doorway into operations, project coordination and management.

Customer support or customer success

What they do. Help customers solve problems by phone, email or chat. Customer success roles go further, helping customers get value over time.

How people enter. Many companies hire for communication and patience and train on the product. Remote roles exist, but check each employer carefully.

Often suits. People who are patient, clear writers and enjoy solving problems for others.

Be honest about. You will sometimes meet upset people, and targets can be demanding. The skills carry well into account management, training and operations.

Digital marketing or social media

What they do. Help organisations get noticed online: planning content, designing posts, writing captions, scheduling, reading simple reports and running small campaigns.

How people enter. Through entry-level assistant roles, internships, volunteering and building a small portfolio of practice work. Free courses can teach the basics.

Often suits. People who mix creativity with curiosity about what works.

Be honest about. Platforms change often, and results can be hard to control. Employers like proof, so build samples early.

Graphic or visual design

What they do. Create visuals that communicate: social graphics, menus, posters, logos, presentations and layouts.

How people enter. Through study, courses or self-teaching with free tools, followed by a portfolio. Many start as freelancers or junior designers.

Often suits. People with a strong eye and patience for revisions.

Be honest about. It is competitive. A niche and a clean portfolio help far more than a long list of tools.

Teaching and training

What they do. Help people learn, in schools, training centres, companies or online. Some roles require formal teaching qualifications and registration. Others, such as tutoring or corporate training, have different entry routes.

How people enter. Check your country's requirements for the exact role. Many people begin with tutoring or classroom assistant work to test whether they enjoy it.

Often suits. People who love explaining, enjoy watching others improve and have patience.

Be honest about. Workloads can be heavy, and pay varies by country and level.

Healthcare support roles

What they do. Support patients and clinical teams. Examples include care assistants, medical receptionists and pharmacy assistants. Clinical roles such as nursing require formal training and registration.

How people enter. Through recognised training and, in some places, entry-level jobs that include training. Always check official sources for qualification rules, because they are strict and vary by country.

Often suits. People who care deeply about helping others and can handle emotionally demanding work.

Be honest about. Hours can be long and shifts irregular. Many people find it deeply meaningful.

Bookkeeping and accounting support

What they do. Record money coming in and going out, prepare invoices, reconcile accounts and help with simple reports. Accounting proper often requires professional qualifications.

How people enter. Through short courses, accounting assistant roles or helping small businesses. Spreadsheet skills and attention to detail are central.

Often suits. People who like accuracy, order and being trusted with important information.

Be honest about. Rules about who may do accounting work and how, vary by country. Check the requirements before you offer services.

Human resources assistant

What they do. Support hiring, onboarding, records, staff questions and workplace processes.

How people enter. Through administrative roles, graduate schemes or entry-level HR positions. Professional certificates can help later.

Often suits. People who are discreet, organised and care about how workplaces treat people.

Be honest about. You will handle confidential information, so trustworthiness is essential.

IT support and basic technology roles

What they do. Help people with computers, accounts, networks and software problems. Other technology roles include data analysis, testing and web support.

How people enter. Through help desk or support jobs, short certificates and self-study with practice. Many technology skills can be learned online for free, with proof built through projects.

Often suits. People who like solving puzzles and learning how systems work.

Be honest about. The field changes quickly, so you must keep learning. Explaining things kindly to non-technical people is a big part of the job.

Skilled trades

What they do. Practical work such as electrical installation, plumbing, carpentry, tailoring, hairdressing, cooking and repair.

How people enter. Often through apprenticeships, vocational training or learning alongside an experienced person. Some trades require licences.

Often suits. People who like working with their hands, seeing tangible results and building independence.

Be honest about. Work can be physically demanding. Skilled tradespeople are often in strong demand, and many eventually run their own businesses.

How to use the snapshots

Choose three that make you curious, and for each, do the fifteen-minute demand check, read five job descriptions and request one informational chat. After that, decide whether to keep it on your list.

12A Sample Informational Conversation

Reading about a conversation helps. Here is a short, made-up exchange between Bisi, who is exploring human resources, and Mrs Okoro, an HR coordinator at a mid-sized company. It is not a script to memorise. It shows the warm, curious rhythm.

Bisi: Thank you so much for your time, Mrs Okoro. I know you are busy. I am exploring careers in HR, and I would love to hear how you got started.

Mrs Okoro: Of course. I began as an administrative assistant in an office, and I ended up helping with staff records. I enjoyed it, so I asked to help with recruitment, and slowly moved into HR.

Bisi: That is really interesting. What does a normal week look like for you?

Mrs Okoro: A lot of emails and scheduling. We have interviews to organise, new staff to onboard, questions from managers about policies and some paperwork. Some days are calm. Other days involve a difficult conversation.

Bisi: What do you enjoy most?

Mrs Okoro: Helping a new person settle in and feel confident. And solving a problem before it becomes a big one.

Bisi: And the hardest part?

Mrs Okoro: Confidentiality. People tell you sensitive things, and you have to handle them carefully. Also, you sometimes have to deliver news that people do not want to hear.

Bisi: What skills matter most?

Mrs Okoro: Communication, discretion, organisation and fairness. Knowing spreadsheets and employment rules helps, and the rules differ by country, so you have to keep learning them.

Bisi: If you were starting again, what would you do first?

Mrs Okoro: I would get an administrative job in a company that has an HR team, and I would volunteer to help them. Then I would study for an HR certificate once I knew I enjoyed it.

Bisi: That is so helpful. Is there anyone else you suggest I speak to?

Mrs Okoro: Yes, I can introduce you to a colleague who recently moved into recruitment.

Bisi: Thank you so much. I will send you a note this evening to say thanks, and I will let you know how it goes.

What Bisi did well

She asked about the person's journey first. She asked specific, open questions. She asked about the hard parts, not only the pleasant ones. She asked "what would you do first?" and "who else should I speak to?", which are two of the most valuable questions you can ask. And she promised a follow-up and kept the promise.

What to write down afterwards

Within an hour, write notes: three things you learned, one thing that surprised you, one thing you liked, one thing that worried you and one action you will take. These notes become the raw material for your decision table.

13Comparing Your Options Fairly

By now you may have a short list: two to four directions that keep appearing. Here is how to compare them without going in circles.

Make a decision table

Draw a table. List your options across the top and your six lenses down the side. Score each option from one to five on each lens, based on what you have learned from research, conversations and experiments. Here is a made-up example.

LensOption A: Digital marketingOption B: TeachingOption C: Healthcare admin
Interests432
Strengths453
Skills I already have343
Values454
Lifestyle fit5 (remote possible)33
Income potential and speed334
Total232319

The scores are made up. The point is what happens next: when two options tie, the table shows you where they differ, and that difference is the real question. In this example, Option A wins on lifestyle and Option B wins on strengths and values. So the decision becomes: "Which matters more to me right now?"

Weigh what matters

Not all lenses matter equally to every person. If income speed is urgent, you may give it double weight. If flexibility matters most, weight lifestyle. You can multiply each score by a weight from one to three before adding. Be honest about your current season of life.

Add three practical questions

Before choosing, answer these for each option:

1. How long until I can earn something? Weeks, months or years? 2. What does it cost to start? Money, time and energy. 3. What is the worst realistic outcome, and could I live with it? If you try it and it does not work, what do you lose, and what do you keep?

The "ten-ten-ten" test

Ask yourself: How will I feel about this choice ten minutes from now, ten months from now and ten years from now? Sometimes a choice that feels frightening today looks wise in ten years, and sometimes the other way round.

Reversible and irreversible choices

Some decisions can be undone easily, like taking a short course. Some are expensive to reverse, like taking on a large loan. Move quickly on reversible choices and slowly on irreversible ones. Most career experiments are reversible, which is wonderful news.

14Education And Training Routes

Many careers have more than one way in. Understanding your options can save you time and money. Rules, costs and recognition differ a lot between countries, so please check what applies where you live.

Formal education

A degree or diploma from a university or college. Required for some careers, such as medicine, law, teaching and engineering. Helpful for others. Usually takes years and can be expensive. Check whether the qualification is recognised, how long it takes, what it costs and what jobs it leads to.

Vocational and technical training

Courses that teach a specific trade or practical skill, such as nursing assistant training, electrical work, hairdressing or IT support. Often shorter and more directly connected to jobs.

Apprenticeships

You work and learn at the same time, often earning a wage. Good for trades and some professional fields. Availability varies by country.

Short courses and certificates

Shorter programmes that teach one skill, from a few weeks to a year. Good for adding a skill or testing an interest. Quality varies enormously, so check reviews, the provider's reputation and whether employers recognise it.

Self-study and free resources

Many digital skills, such as design, writing, spreadsheets, marketing basics and coding, can be learned for free or at low cost online. You will need to build proof through projects, because there may be no certificate. Our free Academy courses on this site are a gentle place to start.

On-the-job training

Some employers hire people with potential and train them. Entry-level roles in customer support, administration and sales often work like this.

Work experience, volunteering and internships

Practical experience can matter more than a qualification in some fields. Volunteering and internships can open doors, but be careful about unpaid work that never ends or that you cannot afford. Check the rules in your country.

Choosing a training provider carefully

Training is a business, and not all of it is honest. Before you pay for any course or programme, ask:

  • Is the provider officially recognised or accredited where required for this career?
  • What do past students say, from sources not controlled by the provider?
  • What exactly will I be able to do at the end?
  • What is the total cost, including exams and materials?
  • Do employers in my area value this training?
  • Is there a refund policy, and can I read it before paying?
  • Do they promise guaranteed jobs or guaranteed income? If so, be very careful.

If something feels pressured or too good to be true, step back.

Paying for training

Look at options in your country: scholarships, bursaries, payment plans, employer sponsorship, government schemes and savings. Be very careful with loans, and understand the total repayment and interest before signing. I am not a financial adviser, so for large decisions please speak to a qualified person.

15Changing Careers

If you already work and want a different direction, welcome. You are in very large company.

First, ask why

Be honest about what you want to leave. Is it the tasks, the company, the manager, the pay, the hours or the whole field? Sometimes the problem is the workplace, not the career. A different employer in the same field may solve it. Sometimes it really is the field. Knowing the difference saves you from a costly change that fixes nothing.

Build a bridge, not a cliff

Instead of quitting and leaping, build a bridge. Keep your income while you explore, learn and test. Use evenings, weekends or a slower season to take a course, do a small project, volunteer or take on a few freelance tasks in the new field. Read What To Build Before Quitting Your 9 To 5 for a careful way to prepare.

Use your transferable skills

Your past experience is not wasted. Translate it. A teacher moving into training and development, a retail manager moving into operations and a customer service worker moving into account management all carry over valuable skills.

Expect a dip

You may start lower in the new field, with lower pay or a more junior title. That is common. Plan for it financially and emotionally, and decide how long you can sustain it.

Tell the story

When people ask "why the change?", have a short, positive answer. "I enjoyed the training part of my job most, so I am moving into learning and development, and here is what I have already done to prepare" sounds purposeful, not flaky.

16Handling Fear And Pressure

Career choices stir up big feelings. Let us face the common ones.

"What if I choose wrong?" Most careers allow movement. Skills transfer. Even a "wrong" choice teaches you what you value. A sensible approach is to pick a direction, test it and adjust.

"My family wants something different." Family expectations can come from love, fear or pride. Listen to the concern behind the words. You can respect their worries without surrendering your choice. A calm line: "I hear that you want me to be secure. Here is my plan, and here is how I will check it works." Show your research, not just your feelings. Remember that you are the one who will live this life.

"I am behind other people." Careers are not races. People start at different ages and from different places. Comparison online is especially unfair, because you see everyone's highlights.

"I am afraid of failing." Failure is information. If an experiment does not work, you have learned something cheaply.

"I do not feel qualified." Few people feel qualified before they start. Qualification grows from doing. Show proof of effort and learning, and apply anyway.

"I have a gap in my CV." Gaps are more common than you think, caused by study, caring, health, relocation or job loss. Explain it briefly and honestly, and focus on what you learned or did in that time.

"I am older than most beginners." Experience is an asset. Many employers value reliability, maturity and judgement.

Pause For A Second 🌸 If the fear feels overwhelming, or if it is mixed with a lot of sadness, please do not carry it alone. Talk to someone you trust, a counsellor or your doctor, depending on what you need. I am not a mental health professional, and looking after yourself comes first.

17How To Decide

At some point you must choose a direction to try. Here is a calm process.

1. Review your fit profile and decision table. 2. Pick the top one or two that excite you and are realistic. 3. Set a test period. Ninety days is a good length. Decide what you will do in that period and what result would tell you "yes, continue." 4. Decide what a "no" looks like. For example, "If I try three small projects and dislike all of them, I will move to my second option." 5. Tell one trusted person your plan and your review date. 6. Start. Take the first small action today.

Notice that this is a decision to test, not a vow for life. That small change removes enormous pressure.

A note on "good enough"

Researchers who study decisions often talk about people who look for the "best" option versus people who look for one that is "good enough." The first group tends to feel more anxious and less satisfied. You do not need the best. You need a good enough direction that you can start, improve and change when needed.

If you still cannot decide

Choose the option that is easiest to start and cheapest to test. Momentum creates clarity. Many people wait for certainty that only arrives after they move.

Clarity usually follows action. It rarely arrives before it.

18Where To Go: Finding People, Advice And Opportunities

Choosing a career is not a solo project. The best information lives in people. In this chapter, I will show you where to find them, platform by platform, and how to behave when you get there. You do not need all of these. Choose your warm network plus two or three others.

Your warm network (start here)

Your warm network is everyone who already knows you: family, friends, classmates, teachers, former colleagues, neighbours, people from your faith or community groups. You probably know more people than you think, and they know people you do not.

Try this: write down fifty names. Next to each, write what they do for work, even if you only know roughly. You will be surprised by how many different careers appear on your own list. Then choose five and message them.

A simple message: "Hi Aunty Ngozi, I hope you are well. I am exploring career options and I know you work in healthcare administration. Would you be willing to chat for fifteen minutes about what your work is really like? I would be so grateful."

LinkedIn

LinkedIn is a professional network where people list their jobs, skills and experience. It is excellent for career research because you can see career paths in real life.

How to use it:

  • Search a job title, and click "People" to see real people with that role. Look at their career paths: what did they do before, and after?
  • Look at the skills and qualifications they list.
  • Follow companies and professionals in fields you are curious about.
  • Read posts to learn how people talk about their work.
  • Send a polite connection request with a short note, then, if they accept, ask for a short conversation.
  • Set up your own profile with a clear photo, a headline saying what you are exploring or learning, and a short "About" section.

Be respectful of people's time, never copy-paste the same message to everyone and never pay anyone who promises to "get you hired."

X (formerly Twitter)

X is a fast, public platform. Many professionals share short lessons, news and opinions about their fields. Follow people in careers you are curious about, read what they share and, when you have something thoughtful to say, reply. Some people have received helpful advice or opportunities this way. Keep your profile professional if you want to be found.

Facebook groups

There are groups for almost every career, city and stage of life. Search for groups about your target field, women in your profession, your city's job seekers or career changers. Read the rules first. Ask clear, specific questions rather than "what should I do with my life?" Answer others when you can. Be wary of groups full of "make money fast" posts.

Instagram

Many professionals share their working days on Instagram. Search hashtags for a job title, such as "day in the life of a nurse," to see the real routine. Follow accounts that show the honest side, not just the glamour. You can also send polite direct messages to people whose work you admire, but keep them short and specific.

TikTok

TikTok is full of short career videos, from "day in my life" clips to explanations of how people entered their fields. Use it to get a feel for different careers, but remember that videos show a highlight reel and may be selective. Verify claims about pay and qualifications through official sources.

Pinterest

Pinterest can be helpful for visual fields, such as design, interior styling, fashion and photography, and for gathering ideas. You can create boards for careers you are exploring, such as "skills to learn" and "portfolio ideas." It is less useful for hard data.

Reddit

Reddit has communities for many careers and for career advice in general. People often share honest experiences, including the downsides. Read community rules and search before asking, because many questions have been answered. Treat individual stories as one person's experience, not as a general rule.

Job boards and freelance marketplaces

Job boards list vacancies, and freelance marketplaces list short-term projects. Even if you are not applying yet, reading listings teaches you what employers want, what titles exist and what skills appear again and again. When you do apply, read each site's rules, check the employer, and never pay to apply.

Local and in-person

Do not forget your own area. Career fairs, school and university careers offices, public libraries, community centres, professional associations, local business meetups and open days can all connect you with real people. Many institutions offer free careers advice or CV help. Ask.

How to choose your two or three

Ask: Where do the people in my target careers already gather? Where can I show up regularly without dreading it? Choose your warm network plus one or two places, and stay for a month before deciding they do not work.

19Scripts You Can Copy

A script removes the blank-screen panic. Every example below is made up. Change the details until it sounds like you.

The kind and legal way to reach out

Be respectful. Send individual, personal messages, not mass copy-paste. Say who you are and why you are writing. Make it easy to say no, and if someone says no or asks you to stop, stop. Rules about unsolicited messages and calls vary by country, so please check local rules, and when unsure, stick to your warm network and to contact details people have published for enquiries.

Script one: asking someone in your network for an informational chat

"Hi Mrs Okafor, I hope you are well. I am exploring careers in accounting and I remember you work in a firm. Would you have fifteen minutes in the next couple of weeks to tell me what your work is really like? I would be very grateful, and I am happy to work around your schedule."

Script two: a LinkedIn connection note to a stranger

"Hello Tolu, I came across your profile while researching careers in UX design. I am considering this path and would really appreciate hearing about your journey. Would you be open to a short conversation? Thank you for considering it."

Keep it under about three hundred characters, because many connection notes have a limit. Check current limits.

Script three: a follow-up message if you hear nothing

"Hi Tolu, I wanted to follow up on my note in case it got buried. No pressure at all, and thank you for your time either way."

Send this once, about a week later. If there is no reply, let it go.

Script four: the questions for an informational chat

Open with thanks. Then ask:

1. "Could you tell me how you got into this work?" 2. "What does a normal week look like for you?" 3. "What do you enjoy most, and what is the hardest part?" 4. "What skills matter most in this role?" 5. "What do you wish you had known when you started?" 6. "If you were starting again today, what would you do first?" 7. "Is there anyone else you think I should speak to?" 8. "Is there anything I can do to help you?"

Script five: the thank-you note

"Thank you so much for your time today. I learned a great deal, especially about [one specific thing]. I am going to [action you will take, such as try a short course]. I will let you know how it goes."

A specific thank-you stands out. People remember it, and sometimes they offer opportunities later.

Script six: asking for work experience or shadowing

"Hello, my name is Ruth. I am exploring a career in [field] and I would love to learn more. Would it be possible to spend a day or a few hours observing, or to help with a small task? I am happy to do whatever is useful. I understand if it is not possible, and thank you for considering it."

Script seven: applying for an entry-level job

"Dear Mr Bello,

I am writing to apply for the Customer Support Assistant role advertised on [site]. I enjoy helping people solve problems, and in my previous role at [place] I handled about [number] customer enquiries a day by phone and message. I am comfortable with email, spreadsheets and learning new systems quickly.

I have attached my CV. I would welcome the chance to talk about how I could contribute to your team.

Thank you for your time.

Kind regards, Ruth Eze"

Keep it short and match it to the exact job. Avoid copying a template word for word.

Script eight: a phone call to ask about opportunities

Use this only where phone contact is appropriate and legal.

"Hello, this is Ruth Eze. Is this a good moment for a quick question? I am interested in working in [field] and I wanted to ask whether you take on entry-level staff or volunteers. If so, who would be the best person to contact?"

If they are busy, ask when to call back, then thank them.

Script nine: answering "no"

"Thank you for letting me know. I appreciate your time. If anything changes, I would be glad to hear from you."

Script ten: talking to family about your plan

"I know you want me to be safe and secure, and I appreciate that. I have researched this carefully. Here is what I have found about the field, the pay and the training. I am going to test it for three months, and I will show you what I learn. Can I count on you to hear me out?"

Tracking your conversations

Use a simple spreadsheet with columns: name, how I know them, career or field, date I messaged, reply, date of conversation, key things I learned, and follow-up. It keeps you organised and shows you your own progress.

20Building A Simple CV And Profile

When you start applying, you need a clear, honest CV and online profile. A CV (curriculum vitae, also called a résumé in some countries) is a one- or two-page document that summarises who you are and what you can do.

What goes in a beginner CV

  • Your name and contact details, with a professional email address.
  • A short summary, two or three lines about who you are and what you are looking for.
  • Skills, including digital skills and transferable skills, with specific examples.
  • Experience, including jobs, volunteering and projects. For each, say what you did and, if you can, what resulted.
  • Education and training, including short courses.
  • Optional: languages, achievements and links to your portfolio.

Writing strong experience lines

Start with a strong verb and say what you did and what happened. "Handled customer questions" is weaker than "Answered about forty customer questions a day by phone and message, and resolved most without escalation." Do not invent numbers, but use real ones when you have them.

Make it easy to read

One clean font, clear headings, plenty of white space and a PDF export. Ask a friend to read it and tell you what stands out. Use the free Resume Review Checklist to catch common mistakes.

Your online profile

Update your LinkedIn or similar profile to match your CV. Use a clear photo, a headline like "Career explorer interested in digital marketing and customer success," and a short summary. Ask people you have worked with for short recommendations if appropriate.

21Interview Basics

An interview is a conversation where an employer or client decides whether to work with you. It is a skill you can practise.

Before the interview

Research the organisation. Read the job description again. Prepare three stories from your experience that show your skills. Plan your journey or test your technology. Prepare two or three questions to ask them.

Common questions and how to answer them

"Tell me about yourself." Give a short summary: who you are, what you have done and why you are interested in this role. Keep it under two minutes.

"Why do you want this job?" Link your interests and strengths to what the role needs. Be specific.

"What are your strengths?" Choose two that match the job, and give a real example of each.

"What is your weakness?" Choose a real, manageable one and say what you are doing about it.

"Tell me about a time you solved a problem." Use the simple structure: the situation, what you did, what happened.

"Do you have any questions for us?" Always ask something, such as "What would a successful first three months look like?"

On the day

Arrive or join early. Greet people warmly. Listen carefully. It is fine to take a moment to think before answering. Be honest, and if you do not know something, say how you would find out.

After the interview

Send a short thank-you message within a day. If you have not heard back by the date they gave you, send one polite follow-up.

If you are rejected

It hurts, and it is normal. Ask politely for feedback, thank them and keep going. Rejections are part of the numbers, not a verdict on your worth.

22A Complete Plan To Turn Your Career Into Income

Choosing a direction is wonderful. But you also need money while you do it. This chapter shows you honestly how a career becomes income, and how to bridge the gap between "I have chosen a direction" and "I am being paid for it." There are no guarantees here. Pay, demand and timelines depend on your country, field, qualifications and effort.

The four ways a career earns

1. Employment. You work for an employer for a salary or hourly wage. This gives stability, benefits in some countries and structure.

2. Freelancing. You sell your skills to several clients on a project basis. This gives flexibility and the chance to earn more, but income can be uneven, and you must find your own clients and handle your own admin.

3. Business. You build a company, shop or practice that sells services or products. This can have the highest ceiling and the highest risk, and it usually takes the longest.

4. A blend. Many people combine a part-time job with freelance work, or a full-time job with a side project. A blend can reduce risk while you test a new direction.

Which route fits your season of life?

If your situation is...A sensible route to consider
I need steady income soonEmployment, or a blend with part-time work
I am a student or have limited hoursPart-time work, internships or small freelance tasks
I want flexibility and have a marketable skillFreelancing, often alongside a job at first
I want independence and can wait for incomeA blend, building a business slowly
I am changing careers while employedKeep your job, build the bridge on the side

The bridge: income while you transition

If you are moving into a new field, you may need income that is not yet in that field. Here is a practical way to think about it.

Layer one: your safe income. A job or work you can rely on to cover essentials. Do not apologise for it. It buys you time.

Layer two: skill-building income. Work that is close to your target and builds experience, such as an entry-level role, a part-time position, a small freelance project or volunteering.

Layer three: the target. The career you are heading toward, with full pay.

You move up the layers gradually. Keeping the bottom layer steady while you build the others is far less stressful than leaping in.

Getting paid in employment

If you are heading toward a job, here is the honest process.

1. Find roles that match your level. Read job titles such as "assistant," "coordinator," "trainee" or "junior." These are entry doors. 2. Tailor your CV to each application. Mirror the language of the job description where it is honest. 3. Apply consistently. Set a weekly target, such as five thoughtful applications. 4. Network in parallel. Many jobs are filled through people, not job boards. 5. Prepare for interviews. Practise out loud. 6. Compare offers carefully. Look at pay, hours, training, growth, workplace culture and benefits. 7. Negotiate respectfully. Many employers expect some negotiation, though customs vary by country. Use the free Salary Negotiation Calculator to prepare your thinking.

Please be careful about what pay is realistic. Look at multiple sources, including official labour statistics for your country, and be cautious with single numbers in videos or ads.

Getting paid through freelancing

If you are heading toward freelance work, the path looks like this:

1. Choose one service connected to your career direction. 2. Build three to five pieces of proof, from practice projects, volunteering and small trials. 3. Set up a simple profile and portfolio. 4. Contact people in your warm network and local area. 5. Offer a clear package at a clear price. 6. Deliver well, ask for testimonials and referrals. 7. Raise your price gradually as your skill grows.

For the full walk-through, read How To Get Your First Freelance Client and How To Get Paid As A Freelancer.

Getting paid through a small business

If you are heading toward a business, start small and test before you spend. Ask: Who is my customer? What problem do I solve? Would someone pay for it? Try a small pilot, such as selling to five people, before investing in anything big. The free Business Idea Validator can help you test your thinking. And please check your country's rules about registering a business, licences and taxes, because they vary widely.

Side income while you explore

Sometimes the best way to test a career is to earn a little in it before committing. Examples, made up for illustration:

  • Someone interested in marketing manages a small shop's social media for a modest monthly fee.
  • Someone interested in teaching tutors a few students in the evenings.
  • Someone interested in design makes flyers and CVs for local people.
  • Someone interested in administration helps a small business with scheduling and email.
  • Someone interested in writing produces product descriptions for small sellers.

Side income does three things at once: it gives you cash, proof and a taste of the real work.

Raising your earning power over time

A career is not static. Here is how people honestly grow their income:

  • Build rare combinations of skills. For example, nursing plus data, marketing plus writing or teaching plus technology.
  • Take on more responsibility, such as leading a small project.
  • Learn skills in demand, keeping an eye on job postings.
  • Show results. Keep a record of what you improved, saved or created.
  • Ask for feedback and for promotions with evidence.
  • Change employers when it makes sense, since moving can sometimes bring higher pay, though not always.
  • Add a side stream, such as freelance work or a small digital product, once you have steady footing. See How To Create And Sell A Digital Product and 35 Semi-Passive Income Streams.

Money habits during a career change

Keep your essentials covered. Build a small emergency fund if you can. Track your spending. Avoid expensive commitments, such as big loans for training, until you have tested the direction cheaply. Keep records of any income you earn. For a full beginner's lesson, read Budget Like A Queen.

I am not a financial adviser, lawyer or tax adviser. Rules about pay, contracts, taxes and benefits differ by country, so please check what applies where you live.

A made-up example of a bridge

Take Amaka, a made-up example. She works in a shop and is curious about digital marketing. Her safe income is her shop salary. Over three months she takes a free introductory course, practises by managing a friend's small business page and talks to two marketing professionals. She finds she enjoys the work. Next she applies for entry-level marketing assistant roles, and offers a small monthly social media package to two local businesses. After six months she moves into a junior marketing role. She did not quit first. She built a bridge and then crossed it.

23Tools And Setup

You do not need much. A short list:

What you needFree option to start with
Notes for your worksheetsA notebook or a notes app
ResearchA search engine and official careers sites for your country
NetworkingLinkedIn and your warm network
CV and documentsA free document tool
TrackingA free spreadsheet
LearningOur free Academy courses and free video tutorials
Online safetyStrong passwords and two-step verification
CalendarA free calendar for your ninety-day review

Check current features, limits and prices before relying on any tool. If you want to strengthen the basics, such as email, files and online safety, read Digital Skills For Beginners.

A simple career folder

Create one folder in cloud storage called "Career." Inside, make subfolders: Worksheets, Research, Conversations, CV and Applications, Certificates, and Learning. Every time you finish an exercise, save it there. Within a month you will have a quiet record of how you think, and it will be useful for interviews, applications and decisions.

A weekly rhythm

  • Explore (two sessions). Research, read job descriptions and watch day-in-the-life videos.
  • Connect (one session). Message or meet one or two people.
  • Test (one session). Do a small experiment, such as a lesson or a practice project.
  • Reflect (ten minutes). Write what you learned.
  • Review (Sunday). Choose three priorities for next week.

24Special Situations: Choosing When Life Is Not Simple

Most career advice quietly assumes a tidy life: no debts, no children, no health limits and a bank of free time. Real life is rarely tidy. Here is how the method bends to fit some common situations.

If you are a student or a recent graduate

You have energy, time to learn and fewer commitments than you may have later. Use your breaks for small experiments: a short internship, volunteering, a part-time job in a field you are curious about or a free online course. Visit your institution's careers office, because many offer free CV reviews and employer contacts. Remember that your degree subject does not lock you in. Many employers care about your skills and attitude as much as your subject.

If you have no degree

Plenty of good careers do not require one, including many trades, digital and administrative roles, sales, customer support and small business. Focus on proof: projects, short courses, references and clear skills. Check each field's requirements, because some, such as healthcare and teaching, have strict qualification rules.

If you are returning to work after a break

A break for caring, health or relocation is not a hole in your value. Write down what you did and learned in that time. Refresh your digital skills, update your CV, and consider a "bridge" role such as part-time, temporary or freelance work to rebuild confidence and recent references. Many employers run return-to-work programmes, so search for them.

If you have caring responsibilities

Flexibility may be your top value, so weigh lifestyle heavily. Look at remote, part-time, shift-based and freelance routes. Be realistic about energy, not only time. Build in rest. A career that works for your whole life is better than one that looks impressive but breaks you.

If you have a health condition or disability

You deserve work that fits you. Think about which tasks, environments and schedules help you do your best work, and look for employers and fields that offer flexibility. Laws that protect workers with disabilities exist in many countries but differ widely, so check your local rules and support services. I am not a medical or legal professional, so for health and rights questions, speak to a qualified person.

If you need money urgently

Be kind to yourself and be practical. Your first job does not have to be your final career. Take work that covers your essentials, then use evenings and weekends for small steps toward a direction you want. Look for roles that offer training or that build skills you can reuse. The three-layer bridge in the income chapter was made for this.

If you are in a country or place with limited jobs

Widen your lens. Look at remote work, but verify every offer carefully, because scams target people who are desperate for work. Look at skills that are needed locally and can be offered to nearby businesses, such as digital help for small shops. Join local business groups and community networks. If moving is an option, research legal, safe and well-documented routes only, and check official government sources. Never pay agents who promise guaranteed overseas jobs, because this is a common scam.

If you feel burnt out

When you are exhausted, big decisions feel impossible, and everything looks grey. Rest first, if you can. Ask whether the problem is the field, the workplace or your workload. Smaller experiments are kinder than big leaps right now. If the exhaustion is deep or lasts, please talk to a doctor or counsellor.

25Questions To Ask Before You Say Yes To A Job Or A Course

When a real opportunity appears, excitement can make us forget to ask the sensible questions. Keep this list somewhere you will see it.

For a job offer

  • What exactly will I do day to day, and who will I report to?
  • What are the hours, the location and any flexibility?
  • What is the pay, how often am I paid and what is deducted?
  • Is the contract written, and have I read all of it? Do I understand the notice period, probation and any restrictions?
  • What training and support will I receive?
  • How are people promoted here, and what do successful people in this role go on to do?
  • What does the team culture feel like? Can I speak to someone who works there?
  • Does this job move me closer to the direction I chose?

Please do not sign a contract you do not understand. For anything serious, ask a trusted, qualified person to read it with you.

For a course or training programme

  • What will I be able to do at the end, and how will I show it?
  • Who teaches it, and what is their experience?
  • What is the total cost, and are there extra fees?
  • How many hours a week will it take?
  • What do former students say, on sites the provider does not control?
  • Is the qualification recognised where I want to work?
  • What happens if I cannot finish? Is there a refund policy?
  • Is the provider pushing me to decide quickly or to pay immediately?

For a freelance or side opportunity

  • Who is the client, and have I checked they are real?
  • What exactly is the work, and when is it due?
  • What is the price, when will I be paid and how?
  • What is included and what is not?
  • Will I gain proof, skills or references that help my direction?

A last check before you commit

Sleep on it. Tell one trusted person. Read it again in the morning. If you feel rushed, that is information. The right opportunities will survive a day of thought.

26Common Mistakes (And How To Dodge Them)

Everyone makes some of these. Seeing them early saves a lot of time.

Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake one is waiting for certainty. You will not feel one hundred percent sure. Test a direction and learn.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake two is choosing only by salary or only by passion. Use all six lenses.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake three is copying someone else's path. Their strengths, values and life are not yours.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake four is relying on quizzes alone. They can spark ideas, but they cannot replace research, conversations and experiments.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake five is ignoring daily reality. Ask what the work looks like on an ordinary Tuesday, not on the best day.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake six is skipping the conversations. One honest fifteen-minute chat can save you a year of guessing.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake seven is paying for expensive training before testing the field cheaply.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake eight is believing "guaranteed job" promises. No honest provider can guarantee employment.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake nine is comparing your beginning with someone else's middle. Compare yourself with who you were last month.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake ten is doing nothing because the choice feels too big. A small action today beats a perfect plan next year.

27When Things Do Not Go To Plan: A Troubleshooting Table

What is happeningWhat it usually meansWhat to try
I do not know what I am interested inYou may not have enough exposureTry three new things, read about five careers and talk to three people
Everything interests me a bitA broad curiosityUse your values and lifestyle lenses to narrow, then test two options
Nothing interests mePossible burnout or low energyRest, talk to someone you trust and start with small experiments instead of big decisions
I keep switching ideas every weekToo much input, no testingChoose one option for ninety days and set review dates
My family disagreesDifferent fears and expectationsShow your research and your test plan, and listen to their concerns
I cannot afford trainingMoney barrierLook for free courses, scholarships, payment plans or entry-level jobs that train you
I have no experienceNormal at the startVolunteer, do practice projects and use transferable skills
Nobody replies to my messagesToo long or genericShorten, personalise and message more people, especially in your warm network
I got rejected from a jobPart of the numbersAsk for feedback, improve your CV and keep applying
I tried something and hated itThat is useful informationWrite what you disliked, and cross it off with a clear conscience
I feel too old or too lateComparison and fearLook at career changers in your field and focus on your transferable skills
I feel stuck in a job I dislikeNeed for a bridgeKeep the job, test a new direction in small ways and set a ninety-day review

28Scam And Safety Warnings

I want you to be hopeful and careful at the same time. Where there are people looking for work, there are people looking to profit from them.

Common scams in career and job searching

  • Fake job offers. High pay, no interview, quick hiring, communication only by chat apps and urgent requests for personal documents.
  • Advance fee scams. Anyone who asks you to pay a fee to get a job, a "placement," "training deposit," "uniform" or "equipment."
  • Fake recruiters. Messages pretending to come from well-known companies, using email addresses that do not match the real company.
  • Guaranteed job courses. Programmes that promise a job or a high salary after paying a large fee.
  • Fake cheque scams. You are sent a cheque or payment for "equipment," told to keep a portion and send the rest back. The original payment later turns out to be fake.
  • Identity theft. Forms that ask for ID numbers, bank details or photos of your documents before you have a verified offer.
  • Career coaching scams. Pushy sellers who promise to reveal your "true calling" for a high price, or who take payment and disappear.
  • "Task" and "like and earn" scams. Easy online tasks that eventually require you to send your own money.

Warning signs

  • Urgency and pressure to decide quickly.
  • Pay that is far too high for the work described.
  • No interview, or only a chat interview.
  • A requirement to pay anything to start.
  • Communication from free email accounts pretending to be a large company.
  • Poor spelling and vague job descriptions.
  • Requests for bank login details, one-time codes or your full ID before a verified contract.

Safety habits

Verify the company independently by typing its official website into your browser, not by clicking a link in the message. Call or email using contact details from the official site. Search the company name with the word "scam" or "reviews." Never pay to be hired. Keep personal documents to yourself until you have a verified offer from a company you have checked. Use strong, unique passwords and two-step verification. Tell someone you trust about any offer that seems unusual.

If you think you have been scammed

Please do not blame yourself. Clever people get tricked every day. Stop contact. If you shared passwords, change them immediately, starting with your email. Contact your bank or payment provider quickly. Save evidence such as screenshots and messages. Report it to the platform and to the appropriate authority in your country. Tell someone you trust.

29Worked Examples

Here are three made-up examples to show how the method works in real life. They are teaching examples, not real results.

Example one: Amaka, the shop worker curious about marketing

Where she starts. Amaka works in a shop. She enjoys talking to customers and making the shop window look good. She does not have a degree.

Fit profile. Interests: social media, design, people. Strengths: communication, creativity. Skills: customer service, basic design on her phone. Values: growth and stability. Lifestyle: prefers some remote flexibility. Income: needs her salary while she tests.

Exploration. She reads ten junior marketing job descriptions. She notices that skills such as social media scheduling, basic design and writing captions appear repeatedly. She speaks to two marketing professionals using the scripts in this guide. They tell her entry-level roles often value initiative and proof of work.

Testing. She offers to run a small bakery's social page for three months, free for the first month and a modest fee after that. She keeps her shop job. She completes a free course and builds a small portfolio.

Decision. At ninety days she reviews: she enjoyed the work, learned fast and got a testimonial. She applies for junior roles and keeps her side client.

Lesson. She did not need a perfect passion. She needed a test.

Example two: Bisi, the graduate with a degree she is unsure about

Where she starts. Bisi finished a degree in a subject she chose to please her parents. She now feels lost.

Fit profile. Interests: psychology, helping people, writing. Strengths: listening, organising. Skills: research, essay writing, spreadsheets. Values: helping, security. Lifestyle: in-person with people. Income: needs a steady wage soon.

Exploration. She lists options: human resources, social work, teaching, counselling, community work and writing. She researches qualification routes in her country and finds that counselling and social work require further training and registration, while human resources assistant roles are entry-level.

Testing. She volunteers at a community organisation two afternoons a week, and speaks to an HR coordinator. She realises she enjoys supporting people through processes more than counselling itself.

Decision. She applies for HR assistant roles, and plans to study for a professional HR certificate once employed, with her employer's support if possible.

Lesson. She learned which part of "helping people" fits her. A degree in one field can open doors in many.

Example three: Ngozi, the mother returning to work

Where she starts. Ngozi stayed home for several years raising children. She wants to return to work with flexible hours and fears she is out of date.

Fit profile. Interests: organisation, community, learning. Strengths: planning, reliability, patience. Skills: budgeting, event coordination, managing a household, basic computer skills. Values: family time, flexibility. Lifestyle: part-time, mostly remote. Income: moderate, starting soon.

Exploration. She researches virtual assistance, administrative support and bookkeeping. She reads Digital Skills For Beginners and works on gaps, such as spreadsheets and email.

Testing. She takes on two small admin tasks for a neighbour's business, charges a modest fee and keeps notes. She practises on practice projects.

Decision. She decides to build a small virtual assistant service part-time, with a plan to apply for part-time admin roles if clients are slow.

Lesson. Her years at home were not a gap in skills. They were a training ground that she learned to describe.

Create your own example

Write your own story in five lines: Where I am now. My fit profile in one sentence. The two directions I will test. The experiment I will do first. The date I will review it.

30Mindset: The Voices That Show Up

When you explore careers, familiar voices appear. Here is how I answer them.

"I should know by now." There is no deadline for knowing. You are allowed to learn as you go.

"I do not want to waste time." Exploring is not wasting time. Not exploring is how people spend ten years in the wrong place.

"Everyone else has it figured out." They do not. Many of them are hiding their confusion, too.

"I am not talented enough." Most careers are built from steady skill and reliability, not from rare genius.

"What if I want to change again?" Then you will, with more skills and more knowledge than before.

"I am afraid to disappoint people." Respect their love, listen to their worries and still make the choice you can live with. Your life is long, and you are the one living it.

You are not late. You are learning where you belong.

31Your First Seven Days: A Gentle Quick Start

About thirty to forty-five minutes a day.

Day 1. Write the six lenses on a page. Do exercise one, the energy list.

Day 2. Do the proud moments list and the curiosity trail.

Day 3. Do the values sort and the ideal week description.

Day 4. Write your income floor, and create your fit profile.

Day 5. Choose two career families, and list five careers to research.

Day 6. Read two job descriptions for each of your top careers. Note repeated skills.

Day 7. Write five names from your warm network, and send your first informational chat message.

32Your Thirty-Day Career Discovery Plan

Here is a full month. About thirty to forty-five minutes a day. If you miss a day, simply continue. There is no penalty.

Week one: know yourself

  • Day 1: Energy list.
  • Day 2: Proud moments and curiosity trail.
  • Day 3: Values sort and ideal week.
  • Day 4: Income floor and target.
  • Day 5: Ask three people what you are good at.
  • Day 6: Write your fit profile.
  • Day 7: Review and choose two career families.

Week two: explore options

  • Day 8: List ten careers in your chosen families.
  • Day 9: Research the first three: daily tasks, requirements, pay and demand.
  • Day 10: Research the next three.
  • Day 11: Read five job descriptions for your top option.
  • Day 12: Read five for your second option.
  • Day 13: Do the fifteen-minute demand check for both.
  • Day 14: Review and shortlist two to four options.

Week three: talk to people

  • Day 15: List fifty people in your warm network and what they do.
  • Day 16: Send three informational chat requests.
  • Day 17: Update your LinkedIn or similar profile.
  • Day 18: Send two messages to professionals outside your network, using the scripts.
  • Day 19: Hold your first conversation and write notes.
  • Day 20: Send thank-you notes.
  • Day 21: Review what you have learned and adjust your shortlist.

Week four: test and decide

  • Day 22: Choose one small experiment for each shortlisted option, such as a short course or a practice project.
  • Day 23: Begin experiment one.
  • Day 24: Continue experiment one and write a short reflection.
  • Day 25: Begin experiment two.
  • Day 26: Continue experiment two and write a short reflection.
  • Day 27: Fill in your decision table.
  • Day 28: Review the ten-ten-ten test and your practical questions.
  • Day 29: Choose your direction for the next ninety days and write what "yes, continue" and "no, switch" would look like.
  • Day 30: Tell one trusted person, write your one-page plan and take your first action.

33Your Ninety-Day Plan

Once you have a direction, here is a three-month structure for testing and building.

Days 1 to 30: learn and build the basics

Complete the thirty-day plan above. By day thirty you should have a fit profile, a shortlist, several conversations, a chosen direction and a plan.

Days 31 to 60: build proof and connections

Take a course or work through free learning for your chosen direction. Create two or three pieces of proof, such as practice projects, volunteer work or small tasks. Update your CV and profile. Have two more conversations with people in the field. Start applying for entry-level roles or offering small services, depending on your route.

Days 61 to 90: earn, review and adjust

Apply consistently, or contact potential clients regularly. Take small paid opportunities if you can. Ask for feedback. At day ninety, do a calm review.

Monthly check-in questions

  • What did I do this month?
  • What did I enjoy and what drained me?
  • What did I learn about the field?
  • Which conversations helped most?
  • Am I closer to being paid for this work?
  • What will I do more of, less of or differently next month?
  • Do I want to continue, adjust or switch direction?

34Questions Girls Ask Me

What if I have no passion at all?

That is very common. You do not need one. Use the six lenses, try small experiments and let interest grow as you get better at something. Many people discover their interests by doing, not by waiting.

What if I like many things?

Then you have options. Use your values, lifestyle and income lenses to narrow down, and test two or three directions in small ways. Many careers combine several interests.

How do I know whether a career quiz result is right?

Treat quizzes as conversation starters. They can suggest ideas, but they cannot know your life, values or circumstances. Check any result against research, real conversations and small tests.

How long should I try a direction before switching?

Ninety days is a good first test period for small experiments. Larger moves, such as long courses, deserve more research first. Decide beforehand what would tell you to continue and what would tell you to switch.

Do I need a degree to have a good career?

Some careers require specific qualifications, and others value skills and proof of work more. Research the requirements for your chosen field in your own country, because rules differ widely.

What if my family wants me to choose a different career?

Listen to the worry behind their words, share your research and your test plan, and make a decision you can live with. You can honour their love without surrendering your choice.

Is it too late to change careers?

Many people change careers in their thirties, forties and beyond. You bring experience and transferable skills. It may take planning and patience, but it is possible.

How do I choose between a stable job and a risky dream?

You do not always have to choose. Build a bridge: keep stable income while you test and build the dream in small ways. Decide in advance what level of risk you can accept and what you would do if it did not work.

Can I have a remote career?

Many careers offer remote or hybrid options, but not all. Check job listings for the roles you are interested in and see how many are remote. Be careful with remote job offers that seem too good to be true.

What if I cannot afford to study?

Look at free courses, scholarships, bursaries, payment plans, apprenticeships and entry-level jobs that offer training. Avoid taking on large debts without careful research and, if possible, advice from a qualified person.

How do I handle rejection?

Treat it as part of the numbers. Ask for feedback politely, improve what you can and keep applying. A rejection is information about a particular role at a particular time, not a judgement of your worth.

What should I do after I choose a direction?

Create a ninety-day plan, build proof, talk to more people and start applying or offering services. Then review and adjust. A career is a long conversation with yourself and the world.

36What To Do Next

You have reached the end of a very long guide, and that tells me something lovely about you: you take your future seriously, and you are brave enough to ask a hard question.

Here is what I want you to carry with you. You do not have to find your one true calling. You have to find a good next step, test it honestly and keep learning. A career is not a single choice you make and then defend for life. It is a path you build, adjust and sometimes turn, using what you know about yourself and what you discover about the world.

So here is your next step, and it is small. Tonight, write the six lenses on a page. Tomorrow, do the energy list. This week, send one message to someone who does work you are curious about. In a month, you will have a fit profile, a shortlist and a real conversation behind you. In three months, you will have tested a direction with your own hands.

When you feel lost, remember that being lost is part of finding. When someone says no, thank them and ask the next person. When someone says yes, show up with your best self.

When you are ready for more, here are some good next steps. Digital Skills For Beginners covers the everyday tools almost every career needs. Best Money-Making Skills To Learn In 2026 compares skills that employers and clients pay for. Personal Branding For Beginners helps people understand who you are and what you offer. What To Build Before Quitting Your 9 To 5 shows how to prepare a safe transition. And our free Academy courses are a gentle place to practise new skills.

I am rooting for you, babe. Begin tonight, go gently and keep going.
